lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.unitTitle: PF2 — Buying Goods and Services: Comparing a Purchase Before You Make It
lessonRef.title: Applied simulation: advertising claims versus verifiable claims

objective: Test an advertising claim against the underlying fictional sale data, compute what the claim implies against what the shopper would actually receive, and rewrite the claim so it is verifiable.
scenario: A fictional store advertises a made-up sale with the headline "Save up to 60%!" The sale data below is invented for this exercise.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional sale data in these directions

tasks.directions: The fictional sale covers 12 items. Exactly 1 of them is discounted 60%. The other 11 are discounted 10%. The item the shopper actually wants has a regular price of $48.00 and is one of the 10% items.

prompts.text: What is the sale price of the item the shopper wants?
What would that same item cost if the headline discount of 60% applied to it?
What is the gap between what the headline suggests and what the shopper would actually pay?

tasks.directions: Now describe the sale as a whole.

prompts.text: What is the average discount across all 12 sale items? Round to one decimal place.
Is the headline claim "Save up to 60%" false as stated?
choices: No, one item is discounted 60%, so the claim is literally true

prompts.text: The headline is literally true and still misleads. Explain how, then rewrite it as a claim a shopper could verify before entering the store.

remediation: If the average discount comes out at 35% — halfway between 10 and 60 — the two rates are being averaged rather than the twelve items. Write out all twelve values, eleven 10s and one 60, and add them before dividing.
extension: Find how many of the 12 items would have to be discounted 60% for the average to reach 30%, and say whether the headline would then be a fair summary.
